request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 74-year-old female admitted with subcutaneous masses, abdominal pain, and fever.

Clinical course: The patient was admitted with several subcutaneous masses, abdominal pain, and fever. Laboratory tests showed an extremely low platelet count, and serum protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal band. Imaging studies revealed subcutaneous masses and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy with moderate splenomegaly. Biopsy of the subcutaneous mass revealed a diagnosis of CSH associated with IgH and Igκ rearrangements, with suspicion of an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder. Further testing of the excised spleen confirmed a diagnosis of DLBCL, non-GCB subtype.

Treatment: The patient underwent laparoscopic splenectomy and was administered eight courses of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. The patient was in partial remission 9 months after diagnosis. PET-CT scan showed resolution of some masses, but serum paraprotein levels remained elevated leading to four cycles of rituximab plus lenalidomide, MG is not visible at one-month follow-up.

Outcome: The patient was evaluated and treated for CSH and DLBCL with rituximab and combination chemotherapy. The patient achieved PR with some improvement in PET-CT scans but elevated serum paraprotein levels; treated subsequently with rituximab plus lenalidomide leading to undetectable MG levels. The patient was discharged to the home for follow-up with routine laboratory tests and imaging scans.
Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The principal diagnosis is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), which is the underlying condition chiefly responsible for the admission. CSH most likely stands for cutaneous (or cutaneous/systemic) lymphoid hyperplasia, a reactive process associated with the lymphoma. The splenectomy and the R-CHOP chemotherapy were both directed at the DLBCL.

In ICD-10-AM, DLBCL is coded to C83.3 (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma), so the three-character category is C83.

CODE: C83
